newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Elections over, Albanians demand lost money back.
newsitem.headline: Elections over, Albanians demand lost money back.

text.p: As the dust settles in Albania after elections, angry investors are demanding compensation for the fortunes they lost in get-rich-quick savings schemes whose collapse ignited months of bloodshed.
Confusion over whether the leader of the newly elected Socialists, Fatos Nano, promised to reimburse investors for their losses during campaigning was adding fuel to the issue.
"Lack of clarity on this is a potential for further political problems," a Western diplomat said.

Fury over the collapse of five shady funds that erased thousands of families' savings triggered off violent uprisings in the impoverished ex-communist nation, forcing President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party government to resign in March.
An election was called on June 29 to calm the unrest, in which over 1,500 died, and the Socialists won by a landslide.

Many of Albania's 3.4 million people, Europe's poorest, blame Berisha and the Democrats for allowing the funds to flourish despite warnings from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank and Albania's central bank.
With the election over, investors have started demanding their money back from the funds, which wiped out an estimated $1.2 billion -- more than half Albania's annual output.
Luftetar Petoshati, a community leader in the southern Albanian town of Vlore which was a centre of protests in January, said reimbursing the money was a priority.
"We don't care who is coming to power. We want our money back otherwise we are ready to resume our protests," Petoshati told the daily Koha Jone on Thursday.
The funds, offering sky-high interest rates, flourished after communism fell in 1990 as new companies scrambled for cash that the tiny banking system could not supply.
Undeterred by the failure of similar schemes in Russia, Romania and Bulgaria, many Albanians sold their houses, sheep and cattle to join the bandwagon.

The schemes proved unusually durable in Albania, which many experts believe was due to money laundering from criminal activities, sanctions-breaking smuggling of petrol to Yugoslavia, and money sent back to Albania from relatives working abroad, estimated at $400 million in 1995.
Although some of the schemes were genuine investment funds, building up businesses, others were pure pyramid funds, simply taking money from new investors to pay the old.
The five major schemes that collapsed -- Sude, Gjallica, Grunasi, Xhaferri and Populli -- hit the more prosperous south hardest, as that was where the majority of investors came from.
The government managed to freeze the bank accounts of two of these, Populli and Xhaferri, which contained $300 million. Investors are getting up to 60 percent of their capital back.

With investors demanding their money, four investment holding companies -- Vefa Holding, Kamberi, Silva, Cenaj & Co -- stopped paying out the initial high interest rates and froze investors' accounts, while paying out small sums.
Nano, a multi-lingual economist who is set to become prime minister when a left-centre Socialist coalition government is appointed shortly, denies promising to repay losses.

"The first step is to analyse with high transparency the situation in collaboration with international organisations and then find a solution on how to compensate people," Nano's spokesman Kastriot Islami told Reuters.
"The promise was to try to compensate people, not reimburse all 100 percent of the money lost. It would be very dangerous to say anything like that as there is no money to give back."

A new law to regulate savings schemes, negotiated with the help of the IMF and World Bank, is expected to be passed once the new parliament is convened after being delayed by political wrangling over essential amendments ahead of the election.
Once in place, the law allows for administrators to be appointed by the government to the remaining schemes and for international auditors to come in to investigate all the funds.
"This will be a very expensive operation but it has to be done," said one Western diplomat.
"No one outside Albania will bail out a government in this position or help the funds, so some solutions have to be found, and the sooner the better."
